                   can sometimes  use to instead of A clause beginning with A to-infinitive when it is clear from the
               context what we are talking about:
                               to come  with you, but |     be able to. (instead of ... to come with you.)
                       It might have been better if Rosa had asked for my help, but she chose not to. (instead of ...
                       chose not to ask for my help.)
               However,  when we  use the verb be in the previous sentence or clause the to-infinitive form of be is
               repeated in the next clause or sentence:
                   ~)  Leon was frightened — or maybe he just pretended to be. (not ... just pretended to.)

             | After most nouns and adjectives that can be followed by A to-infinitive clause, we can leave out the
               to-infinitive clause or use to:
                                 Se   ee Sie              at
                       I’m not going to write another book — at least
                                                                              Also: chance, idea, opportunity,
                       | don’t have any plans (to). (or ... plans to

                       write another book.)
                                                                              delighted, determined
                       ‘Could you and Tom help me move  house?’
                       ‘Well, I’m willing (to), and I’ll ask Tom.’
               We  can also leave out a to-infinitive or use to with some verbs:
                       Alex will collect us by 10 o’clock. He promised (to).
                                                                              Also: agree, ask, begin, refuse,
                       ‘You were supposed to buy some sugar.’ ‘Sorry, |
                                                                              start, try
                       forgot (to).’
                After verbs which must have a complement (i.e. a phrase which completes the meaning of the verb)
               we  can’t leave out to:
                       | admit that | took her watch, but | didn’t mean to.
                                                                              Also: afford, be able, choose,
                       Have you thought about getting vaccinated against
                                                                              deserve, expect, fail, hate,
                       cholera before going there?  certainly advise you to.
                                                                              hope, intend, love, need, prefer

                After want and would like in if-clauses and wh-clauses we can often leave out A to-infinitive or use
           :    to:
                   ©)         welcome to dance if you'd like (to).
                       You can do whatever you would  like (to).
                       Call me Ben jf you want (to).
                       Come  and see us when you want  (to).
                In other clauses (not if- and wh-clauses) we include to:
                     )       planning to see you tomorrow, and | would still like to.
                       1 offered to clean your car because | really want to, not because | hope to be paid.
                In if-clauses and wh-clauses we usually leave out to after like. Compare:
                       You can have one if you like. and You can have one if  like (to).
                       Leave whenever  you like. and Leave whenever you’d like (to).
                However, we include to with negative forms of want, would like, and like, including in if-clauses and
                wh-clauses:
                        ‘Shall we go and visit Laura?’ ‘I don’t really want to.’
                    ©)         have phoned  Jo last night, but it was so late when | got home | didn’t like to.
                    ©)     won't mind you asking him for a loan.’ ‘Oh, no, |      like to.’
